title: The Cat and the Milk (తెలుగు)

full_text:
One season, the granaries of Vijayanagara were overrun by a sudden plague of field mice, threatening the imperial wheat reserves.
King Krishnadevaraya, determined to solve the problem decisively, issued a royal decree:
'Every household in the capital shall be provided with a kitten from the royal catteries and a daily allowance of two cups of fresh, creamy milk from the palace dairy. Each family must raise a fat, vigorous cat to hunt the mice throughout the city!'

Every courtier and citizen gladly accepted the free milk. While their families drank the rich cream, the cats grew pampered, lazy, and ignored the mice completely.

Tenali Raman also received a kitten and the daily supply of milk.
On the very first morning, Tenali poured the fresh milk into a heavy iron bowl and heated it over a blazing charcoal fire until it boiled violently.
He placed the boiling, bubbling milk before the hungry kitten.
The kitten eagerly darted its pink tongue into the liquid—and received an instant, painful scald!
The kitten shrieked, leaped backward, and fled under the cot.

From that day forward, whenever Tenali set down a bowl of milk—even when cooled to ice—the kitten would sniff the bowl from five paces away, puff out its fur in terror, and bolt in the opposite direction!
Tenali fed the cat ordinary scraps of dry roti, fish heads, and water. As a result, the lean, hungry cat roamed the house and granary, catching every mouse within reach!

Months later, King Krishnadevaraya held an imperial parade of the royal cats in the palace courtyard to inspect how well his decree had been fulfilled.
All the courtiers brought forward enormous, round, slumbering cats, bloated with sweet cream.
When mice were released from wicker cages, the pampered cats merely yawned and rolled onto their backs!

Then came Tenali Raman, holding his lean, alert cat on a string.
The King frowned: 'Tenali, thy cat is thin and wiry! Didst thou not give it the royal milk?'
'Maharaj,' replied Tenali with a straight face, 'my cat is a strict ascetic saint. It has taken a sacred vow of total renunciation and refuses to touch even a single drop of milk!'

The King laughed in disbelief: 'A cat that refuses milk? Impossible! Cats love milk more than life itself!'
The King commanded a bowl of sweet, cooled palace milk to be placed before Tenali’s cat.
The moment the bowl touched the tiles, Tenali’s cat took one look at the white liquid, remembered the boiling scald, hissed furiously, and scrambled up the King's velvet throne canopy to get away from the bowl!

The King and the courtiers stared in utter astonishment.
Tenali smiled gently:
'Your Majesty, a creature that is given too much comfort forgets its nature and purpose. The courtiers' cats grew fat on royal charity and caught no mice, while my cat, kept alert by simple fare, cleared the granaries. When rulers shower unearned luxuries upon their servants, they create idle parasites who run from their duty.'

Krishnadevaraya grasped the profound administrative lesson beneath the comedy, rewarded Tenali with a purse of gold, and revised the city’s granary policies with practical wisdom.
moral: True governance cannot be forced by unthinking decrees; blind obedience exposes the folly of impractical mandates. [TE]
